paragraphs: The paper studies two proposed functions of the prefrontal cortex: maintaining information temporarily and inhibiting responses. The authors develop a behavioral task and a computational model together, so that the task probes both functions and the resulting behavior constrains the model. This connects the model’s internal processing to observable actions rather than treating memory and inhibition as isolated abilities.

The model operates in continuous time. That makes the timing of processing part of the explanation, allowing the authors to examine how activity unfolds during the task. The behavioral data therefore provide a way to assess a dynamic account of how the two proposed prefrontal functions interact.

The authors also use the model to explore how neuromodulation could change behavior. In particular, they derive testable predictions about schizophrenia under the hypothesis of reduced dopamine influence in the prefrontal cortex. These are predictions conditional on that biological hypothesis, linking a proposed change in brain function to consequences that could be examined behaviorally.
neurips-1994-a-computational-model-of-pr.tldr: A continuous-time model links prefrontal memory and inhibition to behavior and generates predictions about reduced dopamine influence.

paragraphs: The paper compares more than ten prominent models of orientation and ocular dominance columns in visual cortex. Some models describe the spatial patterns themselves, while others explain how those patterns develop through activity. Evaluating both kinds together helps separate a model’s descriptive success from its proposed account of formation.

The authors implement the models on parallel computers, explore their parameter settings extensively, and compare predictions quantitatively with optical measurements from macaque visual cortex. This makes the comparison broader than checking whether one selected output looks convincing. It examines how well the proposed mechanisms account for measured cortical organization across explored settings.

Many apparently different models turn out to share underlying principles and consequently produce similar predictions. Certain pattern models and developmental correlation-based learning models disagree with the measurements. Among the models investigated, competitive Hebbian approaches and Swindale’s model provide the closest agreement. The finding favors those approaches within the comparison while also showing that differences in model presentation need not imply differences in explanatory behavior.
neurips-1994-a-critical-comparison-of-mo.tldr: A quantitative comparison of cortical-column models finds shared principles and identifies competitive Hebbian models and Swindale’s model as the best matches tested.

paragraphs: The paper explores decoding compressed block data by allowing a physical system to settle into a solution. Starting from a decompression algorithm for fractal block codes, the authors construct a recurrent neural network using simple analog circuit models. The circuit dynamics perform the computation through their evolution toward a stable state.

The neuron and synapse models are strongly nonlinear, and the resulting system has many fixed points: states at which it could remain unchanged. The crucial contribution is a parameter-selection procedure that makes only the desired solution stable. This distinguishes the existence of a possible solution from the stability needed for the physical decoder to reach a useful outcome.

As a partial demonstration, the authors present measurements from a 16-neuron analog CMOS chip operating in the subthreshold regime. For each parameter choice, it converges to a unique stable state with a qualitatively fractal shape. These observations support the proposed connection between fractal decoding and analog dynamics, while the paper explicitly presents the small chip as a partial proof of concept.
neurips-1994-an-analog-neural-network-in.tldr: A small analog recurrent network demonstrates how carefully chosen dynamics can settle into a stable solution inspired by fractal decompression.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a comparison problem in recurrent neural network research: many discrete-time architectures had been proposed, but little experimental work had examined them together. The authors review and categorize these architectures before comparing their performance. This gives the study both an organizing role and an empirical one.

The experiments cover several classes of simple problems, including grammatical inference and nonlinear system identification. These represent different kinds of sequential learning: discovering structure in sequences and learning the behavior of a changing system. Including both makes the comparison relevant to more than a single use of recurrence.

The approach matters because proposing a recurrent architecture and understanding how it behaves across tasks are separate contributions. Categorization provides a framework for relating design alternatives, while experiments connect those alternatives to actual learning problems. The abstract presents the scope and purpose of this comparison without naming a winning architecture. Its central contribution is therefore a systematic empirical examination of recurrent designs across different problem classes.
neurips-1994-an-experimental-comparison-.tldr: The paper organizes recurrent network architectures and experimentally compares them on simple sequence-learning and system-identification problems.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether diversity in neuronal responses can explain aspects of cortical organization. The proposed organizing principle is that the arrangement of connections promotes a varied collection of response properties. The authors connect this idea to the relative sizes of dendritic and axonal branching structures, linking anatomical geometry to the information neurons can represent.

Their analysis finds that response diversity is maximized when dendritic and axonal arbor sizes have a ratio of one. The supplied evidence notes that similar size matching occurs in multiple cortical areas and species. This agreement gives the diversity principle a specific anatomical consequence, beyond a general preference for varied neural responses.

The authors also examine what that diversity contributes computationally. Maximizing it improves performance in receptive-field systems implementing steerable or shiftable filters and in matching signals distributed across space. These results connect anatomical organization, response variety, and visual computation. The contribution is the argument that diversity can both correspond to observed structure and improve the operations that such structures support.
neurips-1994-anatomical-origin-and-compu.tldr: The paper links matched axonal and dendritic sizes to maximal response diversity and improved visual computations.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a statistical-mechanics framework for modeling discrete time series. Its models, called Boltzmann chains, are one-dimensional networks whose weights are shared across the chain. Training uses Boltzmann learning to maximize likelihood. Hidden Markov models fit within this framework as a special case, giving the new formulation a direct connection to an established sequence model.

The framework also motivates two architectures designed around specific sequence-modeling needs. Parallel chains represent groups of features that change at different time scales. Looped networks represent dependencies between hidden states over longer intervals. These extensions make the organization of the model reflect distinct kinds of temporal structure.

For these architectures, the authors show how to carry out the Boltzmann learning rule exactly in polynomial time. The required calculations use exact decimation procedures from statistical mechanics rather than simulated or mean-field annealing. This is central to the contribution: the paper expands the available sequence structures while providing exact learning computations for the particular networks it studies.
neurips-1994-boltzmann-chains-and-hidden.tldr: Boltzmann chains generalize hidden Markov models and enable exact learning for architectures addressing multiple time scales and long-term dependencies.

paragraphs: The paper connects probabilistic classification with clustering-based decision rules. It starts from a Bayes classifier whose distribution for each class is represented by a mixture of Gaussians. The authors then derive winner-take-all approximations, which use a winning component in place of the fuller mixture calculation. This provides a probabilistic route to simpler classifiers.

The derived family includes clustering approaches such as learning vector quantization and k-means. Relating these methods through a common starting point helps explain how cluster-based decisions can approximate decisions based on class probability models. The authors also propose a Gaussian mixture model with a rank constraint and derive a corresponding winner-take-all algorithm.

Experiments on two speech classification tasks indicate that the constrained model and the winner-take-all approximations improve performance over unconstrained models. In these tests, simplifying the decision procedure and restricting the model do not merely make it different; they improve classification. The result supports examining model structure and approximation together when designing a classifier.
neurips-1994-classifying-with-gaussian-m.tldr: Winner-take-all approximations connect Gaussian-mixture classification to clustering and improve results on two speech tasks alongside a constrained-rank model.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to combine several estimators when their usefulness varies with the input. Instead of assigning each estimator one fixed weight, it makes the weights functions of the current input. The resulting combination can give different estimators more influence in different parts of the input space.

The authors derive two ways to determine those weights. One evaluates how each estimator’s variance depends on the input. The other estimates how likely the estimator is to have encountered data near the current example. The second approach is closely related to mixtures of experts, and the paper derives learning rules for that setting using ideas from learning with missing features.

A practical feature of the approach is modularity. When another estimator is added, the weighting functions can be modified without retraining. The framework also accommodates estimators that were not learned from data, including expert systems and algorithms. Its contribution is therefore both a rationale for input-dependent weighting and a way to combine heterogeneous sources of estimates.
neurips-1994-combining-estimators-using-.tldr: Input-dependent weights combine estimators according to local uncertainty or data familiarity while allowing modular additions.

paragraphs: The paper studies how people generalize when learning a changed relationship between visual locations and movements. Using computer-controlled alterations of visual feedback, the authors modify selected input-output relationships in the visuomotor map. They then examine how those changes affect other locations and how learning depends on the movement’s starting point.

Changing only one or two relationships produces a significant change across the map, with the effect diminishing away from the remapped locations. The authors interpret this broad but decaying generalization as evidence for representational units with large functional receptive fields. A local learning experience therefore influences a wider range of movements.

The context-dependent experiments show that one visual location can become associated with two finger locations, depending on where the movement begins. As the starting context changes, behavior shifts gradually between the learned mappings. This is consistent with two visuomotor modules whose influence is smoothly controlled by context. Together, the findings use generalization patterns to infer possible computational organization underlying movement learning.
neurips-1994-computational-structure-of-.tldr: Visuomotor remapping spreads beyond trained locations and shifts smoothly with context, suggesting broad representations and context-gated modules.

paragraphs: The paper examines why Markovian sequence models can struggle to learn relationships between events separated by long intervals. Its focus is diffusion: as transitions accumulate, the information needed to connect later outcomes to earlier states becomes dispersed. That makes assigning learning credit across a long sequence difficult, including in hidden Markov models.

Using results from Markov chain theory, the authors show that diffusion decreases when transition probabilities approach zero or one. Such transitions are closer to definite choices than uncertain branching. The result identifies a structural condition that can help preserve the distinctions needed to learn dependencies over longer spans.

That condition has different consequences for different model families. Standard hidden Markov models have very restricted modeling capabilities when their transitions become nearly deterministic. Input/output hidden Markov models can still perform useful computations in this regime. The paper therefore identifies both a way to reduce diffusion and a tradeoff: preserving temporal credit can constrain what a model expresses, with the severity depending on its architecture.
neurips-1994-diffusion-of-credit-in-mark.tldr: Nearly deterministic transitions reduce credit diffusion, but their effect on modeling capacity differs between standard and input/output HMMs.

paragraphs: The paper considers how a neural network can learn the dynamics behind a time series. Its central argument is that training should evaluate predictions over multiple steps. When a predictor is repeatedly applied, its outputs form a trajectory, so learning should constrain the behavior of that iterated model as well as individual predictions.

The authors implement this idea using a recurrent neural network trained through trajectory learning. The training target is a sequence of future behavior rather than only the next observation. This directly connects the learning problem to the intended use of the model: generating an evolving account of the underlying system.

For chaotic time series, the paper also presents a way to choose the trajectory length used in training. That choice determines the span over which the iterated predictor is constrained. Experimental results support the proposed method. The contribution combines an argument for multistep training, a recurrent implementation, and a procedure for selecting the training horizon in the chaotic setting.
neurips-1994-dynamic-modelling-of-chaoti.tldr: Training recurrent networks on multistep trajectories helps constrain learned dynamics, with a trajectory-length selection method for chaotic series.

paragraphs: The paper addresses incomplete input vectors both while a supervised network is learning and when it makes predictions. The authors approximate the distribution of inputs using Parzen windows, a method for representing a distribution from data. That approximation supplies a basis for handling unknown feature values within the learning and prediction procedures.

For prediction, the paper derives closed-form solutions for arbitrary feedforward networks. For training, it approximates the backpropagation update for an incomplete example through a weighted average of backpropagation updates. The common idea is to make missing-input handling part of the computation, using the estimated input distribution to inform the result.

The stated computational advantage is that the complexity of these training and prediction solutions does not depend on how many features are missing. This addresses the concern that increasingly incomplete vectors could make processing progressively more expensive. The authors verify their theoretical results on one classification problem and one regression problem, covering both discrete decisions and continuous-valued predictions.
neurips-1994-efficient-methods-for-deali.tldr: A Parzen-window input model enables efficient prediction and approximate backpropagation with incomplete feature vectors.

paragraphs: The paper examines a problem with using expert image labels as ground truth: visual judgments can be noisy and biased. In remote sensing, these judgments may guide both the training of recognition algorithms and the assessment of their performance. Treating them as unquestionable truth can therefore affect what is learned and how success is measured.

The authors study this issue while detecting small volcanoes in radar images of Venus collected by Magellan. Their work focuses on calibrating the reliability and bias of human labelers. They use the Expectation-Maximization procedure in empirical analyses that account for the subjective nature of the labels.

The reported results suggest that modeling this noise can substantially affect estimates of both human and algorithmic detection performance. The contribution concerns the reference standard as much as the detector: an observed disagreement need not automatically establish which judgment is wrong. Accounting for uncertainty in the labels offers a more informative basis for interpreting detection results in this application.
neurips-1994-inferring-ground-truth-from.tldr: Modeling expert-label noise changes how human and algorithmic volcano detection performance is assessed in Venus radar images.

paragraphs: The paper tackles unsupervised learning of object-level representations. Its starting point is coherence: related sensory observations can remain consistent across time, space, or different modalities. Encouraging agreement between groups of units receiving separated inputs can turn that consistency into a learning signal, helping a network discover structure beyond low-level features.

The proposed procedure simplifies this agreement-based approach. It learns features in a single-layer network containing several populations of units and can also train multilayer networks one layer at a time. This provides a route for applying the same learning principle to hidden representations as well as final outputs.

When trained on sequences of moving geometric objects, a two-layer network learns accurate object classification that is insensitive to position. The finding shows how temporal coherence can support learning what remains consistent while an object moves. The underlying assumption is that sensory coherence contains useful information about object identity; the demonstrated result uses moving geometric objects to put that principle into practice.
neurips-1994-jpmax-learning-to-recognize.tldr: An unsupervised agreement-based learning procedure uses moving-image coherence to learn position-invariant object classification.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the computational cost of recognizing handwritten characters with tangent distance. This distance measure incorporates invariance to selected transformations, allowing nearest-neighbor classification to account for changes that should preserve character identity. The difficulty is that a classifier may need to store and compare against a very large collection of prototypes.

The authors develop richer models that each represent substantial subsets of those prototypes. The aim is to replace many individual reference examples with representations that capture their shared structure. This shifts attention from the distance calculation alone to the way the classifier organizes and represents its reference collection.

The proposed models can be used in two ways: as one model per class or as building blocks combined with k-means clustering. These options allow representation at either the whole-class level or through multiple groups within a class. The contribution is a modeling strategy aimed at the time and memory burden of tangent-distance classification while retaining its emphasis on transformation-aware comparisons.
neurips-1994-learning-prototype-models-f.tldr: Rich prototype models represent groups of handwritten examples to address the storage and comparison costs of tangent-distance classification.

paragraphs: The paper studies product units, which allow a neural network to learn higher-order combinations of its inputs. Such combinations can express interactions that are useful for efficient learning. However, the authors show that ordinary backpropagation encounters difficulties when training networks containing these units, making their representational promise difficult to realize directly.

They investigate those learning problems and propose unconventional heuristics to improve training. Using the heuristics, they introduce a constructive method that builds networks capable of solving well-studied problems with substantially fewer neurons than previously reported. The result connects training choices to the compactness of the resulting representation.

The authors also add product units as candidate units within Cascade Correlation, allowing the constructive system to consider them as it grows a network. In this setting, the networks are smaller and train faster than versions using sigmoidal or Gaussian units. The findings suggest that product units become more useful when paired with learning procedures suited to their particular training behavior.
neurips-1994-learning-with-product-units.tldr: Specialized training heuristics and constructive learning make product units yield smaller networks, with faster training in Cascade Correlation.

paragraphs: The paper represents a biological neuron through its transformation of incoming events into outgoing spikes. Inputs arrive as time-varying postsynaptic activations across the dendrites, while the output is a single sequence of action potentials. The authors design the Spatio-Temporal Event Mapping architecture, or STEM, to learn this relationship from biophysical neuron models.

A trained network, called a STEM cell, can replace a conventional compartmental model when the simulation only needs the neuron’s input-output behavior. This is the stated condition for substitution. The learned model preserves the relevant mapping for that purpose without requiring the simulation to use the original compartmental representation.

The authors identify advantages in computational efficiency, ease of mathematical analysis, and suitability as a framework for VLSI implementations. Network simulations are a motivating application because they can depend on how neurons respond to one another’s signals. The contribution is a trainable temporal abstraction of a neuron, with its usefulness tied explicitly to simulations where the transfer function is what matters.
neurips-1994-model-of-a-biological-neuro.tldr: STEM learns a neuron’s temporal input-output mapping as an efficient substitute when simulations require only its transfer function.

paragraphs: The paper approaches speech coding through the problem of modeling speech. It uses a hierarchical mixture of experts to predict parameterized speech over short time intervals. The model combines local predictions, making the predictor’s organization part of its statistical description rather than treating prediction solely as an input-output calculation.

The authors emphasize two advantages over traditional nonlinear approximators such as multilayer perceptrons: a statistical account of how the predictor operates and information about its performance through likelihoods and local error bars. These outputs describe more than a predicted value. They provide a way to examine how well the model accounts for observations and how uncertainty varies locally.

The paper studies these properties on synthetic and real regression and time-series problems. It also extends the local-combination principle to vector quantization for speech coding. In that scheme, fixed local codebooks are combined online for each observation. This carries the mixture approach from predicting acoustic vectors into adapting the representation used to encode them.
neurips-1994-non-linear-prediction-of-ac.tldr: Hierarchical mixtures of experts provide speech predictions with local uncertainty information and motivate observation-dependent combinations of quantization codebooks.

paragraphs: The paper asks what representation of sound is suitable for modeling human hearing. It argues that representations successful on many single-speaker engineering tasks may be insufficient for harder auditory problems. Its focus is the correlogram, a nonlinear sound representation that the authors describe as plausible in terms of auditory neurophysiology.

The central contribution is showing how to convert this representation back into sound. This inversion matters because it connects an internal representation to an audible result: the reconstructed sound reveals whether perceptually important information has survived the transformation. The authors report that correlogram inversion preserves such information.

The work also presents improved inversion methods for spectrograms and for a cochlear model. Together, these methods extend pattern playback across several representations used to describe auditory processing. The claim about the correlogram concerns preservation of perceptually important information, rather than an explicitly stated requirement of exact waveform recovery. The paper thus makes a richer auditory representation usable in both directions, from sound into a model and back into sound.
neurips-1994-pattern-playback-in-the-90s.tldr: The paper reconstructs sound from correlograms without losing perceptually important information and improves inversion of other auditory representations.

paragraphs: The paper reframes recurrent network training as learning the dynamics of a system in phase space. A point in this space represents a system state, and a vector field describes how that state changes. Under this view, training seeks a match between the network’s dynamics and those of the process being modeled.

The authors use phase-space reconstruction to make hidden states explicit. With those states available, temporal learning becomes a feedforward prediction problem: learn how an explicit state evolves, then repeatedly apply the learned prediction. They advocate this iterated-prediction approach for deterministic signals, which is the stated setting for their training proposal.

The framework is presented as supporting several related goals: learning multiple trajectories, ensuring their stability, and designing dynamical systems. These goals concern the behavior produced by repeated prediction, not just isolated outputs. The contribution is therefore a way to organize recurrent learning around state-space structure, making trajectories and stability direct objects of training and design.
neurips-1994-phase-space-learning-89462f.tldr: Phase-space reconstruction turns learning deterministic recurrent dynamics into explicit-state prediction, supporting trajectory learning and stability.

paragraphs: The paper uses neural prediction to compress text. A network observes a fixed number of preceding characters and estimates the probability of each possible next character. Its task is therefore to produce a distribution over what could follow, rather than simply choosing one character as the most likely continuation.

Those probabilities are passed to standard coding algorithms. Characters assigned high probability receive shorter codes, while surprising characters receive longer ones. This connects the quality of the learned language prediction to the amount of space needed for encoding: the predictor supplies expectations, and the coding procedure converts them into variable-length representations.

On short German newspaper articles, the method outperforms widely used Lempel-Ziv approaches associated with compress and gzip. That is the stated experimental setting for the comparison. The contribution shows that a neural estimate of character-level context can be useful as part of a practical compression pipeline, with the network handling probability estimation and an established coder handling the representation of those predictions.
neurips-1994-predictive-coding-with-neur.tldr: A neural next-character predictor drives text coding and outperforms common Lempel-Ziv methods on short German newspaper articles.

paragraphs: The paper recognizes handwritten digits using a mixture of locally linear generative models of pixel images. Multiple models for the same digit represent different writing styles. To classify a new image, the system evaluates its log-likelihood under the models, asking how well each learned explanation accounts for the observed pixels.

Training uses an Expectation-Maximization algorithm whose model-update step is principal components analysis. This makes the update computationally straightforward while allowing a class to contain several local descriptions. The combination accommodates variation within a digit category without requiring one linear model to represent every style of handwriting.

The authors also incorporate information about expected small deformations through tangent planes. They do this by adding tangent vectors to the sample covariance matrices used by PCA, connecting transformation information directly to the existing training calculation. This addition improves recognition performance. The result shows that a mixture of simple local models can benefit from explicitly representing how an image may change while retaining its digit identity.
neurips-1994-recognizing-handwritten-dig.tldr: Mixtures of local linear digit models capture writing styles, and adding deformation information to PCA improves recognition.

paragraphs: The paper proposes an oscillator network for grouping parts of an input into separate patterns. Each unit is a relaxation oscillator with two time scales. Connections provide local excitation and global inhibition, creating a system in which nearby related activity can be encouraged while competing activity is suppressed across the network.

Its central mechanism is selective gating. When one oscillator enters its active phase, it rapidly recruits oscillators driven by the same pattern and prevents others from activating at that moment. The authors analytically show that this produces synchronization within blocks stimulated by connected regions and desynchronization between different blocks.

Computer simulations demonstrate promising real-time segmentation of multiple input patterns. The timing relationships serve two complementary purposes: shared timing groups a region’s elements, while separated timing distinguishes different regions. The authors present the model as a physical basis for oscillatory accounts of feature binding and as a possible computational framework for scene segmentation and separating figures from their backgrounds.
neurips-1994-synchrony-and-desynchrony-i.tldr: Local excitation and global inhibition synchronize oscillators within patterns while separating different patterns in time.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the difficulty of understanding electrical signaling from a neuron’s anatomical shape. The spatial distribution and timing of voltages matter for neuronal function, but a picture of the cell’s branches does not directly express how signals attenuate. The authors develop a transformation intended to make that relationship quantitative and intuitive.

The method maps the cell’s architecture from anatomical space into electrotonic space. Its distance measure is based on the logarithm of voltage attenuation. Consequently, distances in the transformed representation describe electrical weakening rather than simply physical separation. The representation changes what it means for two locations in the neuron to be electrically close or distant.

The authors explain the theory underlying the transformation and illustrate its use. Its contribution is an analytical view of neuronal structure organized around signal propagation. By making attenuation part of the geometry, the method offers a way to reason about the functional consequences of form using a representation directly tied to electrical behavior.
neurips-1994-the-electrotonic-transforma.tldr: The electrotonic transformation redraws neuronal structure using voltage attenuation as distance to clarify the connection between anatomy and signaling.

paragraphs: The paper adapts multilayer perceptrons to the Intel Ni1000, a parallel neural-network chip built to compute city-block distances. These distances add absolute differences between input values and stored weights. Conventional perceptron calculations depend on dot products, creating a mismatch between the algorithm’s central operation and the computation supported efficiently by the hardware.

The authors address this by expressing Euclidean dot products through Euclidean norms, then approximating those norms with city-block norms. The approximation uses a property of high-dimensional spaces. This reformulation produces a City Block MLP that can use the chip’s parallel architecture without requiring its ordinary dot-product computation.

The approach enables throughput on the order of 40,000 classifications per second for 256-dimensional inputs. The supplied evidence also reports that the City Block MLP performs well on handwritten-character and human-face recognition data. The contribution is an algorithm-hardware adaptation: changing the mathematical form of the network’s calculation makes an existing parallel chip useful for a broader class of neural methods.
neurips-1994-the-ni1000-high-speed-paral.tldr: Approximating dot products with city-block calculations lets multilayer perceptrons exploit the Ni1000’s fast parallel hardware.
